Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: I have to be on guard all the time
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

issues.item: Triggers: Being Praised: Receiving praise or positive attention
issues.explanation: 'Being praised' is a hard-to-explain trigger in a profile otherwise centered on a life-threatening accident with sensory trigger cues, intrusive reliving, and hypervigilant threat monitoring. Unlike smell or darkness, praise has no evident link to the accident-based memory/threat pattern and stands out as clinically incoherent unless additional interpersonal trauma context were present.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: 'Institutional failure' fits betrayal, assault, military, or disaster-response contexts more naturally than a single life-threatening accident in a financial analyst. In this profile the other appraisals focus on danger and inability to cope; this item introduces a qualitatively different blame/betrayal theme that is not supported by the trauma type, trigger pattern, or memory content.

vignette: Tane, a 63-year-old Māori financial analyst, has lived most of his adult life crunching numbers for a large investment firm in Wellington. In late October 2019, he was driving home after a long meeting when a sudden burst of fog reduced visibility to a few meters. His headlights flickered; a slick patch on the road betrayed an unseen puddle. At the instant his car met the wet asphalt, the steering wheel tore out of his hands. The vehicle skidded, struck a tree, and the impact sent a surge of hot, acrid oil fumes up into the cabin. The dashboard shattered, and the sudden darkness of the night pressed in around him, making every turn of his head feel like he was inside a coffin. The thudding, metallic crash sound was so loud that it reverberated through his bones. He emerged from the wreckage disoriented, coughing and choking on the smell of burnt rubber and oil, his heart hammering in a way that seemed to precede his thoughts. The event left him with a life-threatening injury, a broken collarbone, and a memory that feels as present now as it did that fateful night. Within days, Tane noticed that the very scent of gasoline, the murky darkness of a poorly lit hallway, or even a distant honking horn could lift the heavy weight of that night into his present. Those triggers set off the same disorienting, present-feel memory: he would hear the screeching tires, feel his body tighten, and the crash would seem to re-unfold before his eyes. The intrusive memory would then send a surge of fear so intense that his body responded before his mind could calm him. In those moments he would find himself waking mid-night, heart racing, clutching his pillow as if to brace for another crash, only to discover the room around him was empty. These episodes were accompanied by a hypervigilant sense that he must constantly scan for exits, a compulsion that began the moment he stepped into any office building or even the living room of his home. The memory's vividness, coupled with the sensory triggers, reinforced his belief that he could never be safe; the very thought of the accident seemed to doom him. In this way, triggers gave rise to the painful memory, and the memory intensified his perception of threat. The relationship among these elements tightened into a reinforcing loop. Every time a trigger emerged, it dredged up the memory, and the memory, in turn, made Tane feel the body's immediate fight-or-flight reaction. That bodily response amplified the sense of danger so that he began to view every situation as potentially life-threatening. His thoughts became a battleground: if he entertained the memory, he would feel overwhelmed; if he avoided thinking about it, he felt helpless and powerless. Thus, negative appraisals-his conviction that he must remain on guard, his belief that thinking about the crash would break him, and his constant vigilance over future threats-fed directly into the sensation of danger itself. These appraisals also made him more likely to notice triggers, heightening the probability that a sudden smell or a dark corner would launch the full memory into his present. Consequently, the loop grew tighter, each element feeding the next: triggers spurred memory and negative appraisals; negative appraisals amplified threat and brought memory back; memory heightened threat and rekindled triggers; threat itself made every new stimulus feel ominous. The chain was self-reinforcing, and over months it spilled over into Tane's professional life. At the firm, Tane found himself avoiding the stairwell that led to the third floor, preferring instead to call the receptionist for a lift. When his manager asked him to present a quarterly report in a dimly lit conference room, he declined, insisting that the low lighting would provoke a flashback. His colleagues began to notice his withdrawn manner; the stress of constant scanning and the anxiety of potential danger made his concentration on complex financial models erratic. The fear of a new accident haunted his every decision: would the ceiling collapse? would a sudden car sound startle him in the hallway? Because of this, Tane began missing deadlines and his supervisor grew concerned. At home, his wife, Lani, grew frustrated with his avoidance of the living room at night, insisting that the bedroom's dim lighting would keep the house safe, but Tane would refuse, fearing the darkness could trigger the memory. Their conversations often ended with Tane insisting that staying away from the darkness was the only way to keep their lives from ending abruptly. After years of navigating a maze of sensory triggers and intrusive memories, Tane's relationship with his work suffered to the point that he had to take an extended leave of absence. The persistent, body-first reaction to perceived danger, the overwhelming sense that he could not control the environment, and the loss of his professional confidence culminated in a decision to seek help. He arrived at the clinic exhausted, telling the therapist that the most frightening thing was the possibility that he would lose his life again, that a sudden car horn or the faint smell of gasoline could turn a quiet evening into a disaster. Yet beneath that fear, there was a glimmer of hope: he longed to reclaim his mornings, to sit at his desk without scanning for exits, and to finally breathe without the constant sense that his body was ready to run or fight at any moment.
